questions.question: How does Spring's @Scheduled work, what are the differences between fixedRate, fixedDelay, cron, and how do you make it safe in clustered deployments?
questions.title: Spring @Scheduled — fixedRate vs fixedDelay vs cron, plus Clustered Patterns
questions.direct_answer: Enable with **`@EnableScheduling`**; annotate methods with **`@Scheduled`** specifying one of: **`fixedRate`** (time between start times — overlap possible if task is slow), **`fixedDelay`** (time between end-of-last and next start — never overlaps), or **`cron`** (time-of-day expressions). The default thread pool is **single-threaded**; configure a `TaskScheduler` with adequate threads or tasks block each other. In **clustered deployments** `@Scheduled` fires on every replica — use **ShedLock**, **Quartz clustered**, or **Kubernetes CronJob** for single execution. Keep tasks **idempotent**, short, and observable.

interviewer_intent.testing: Thorough understanding of `@Scheduled` timing semantics, thread-pool config, and clustered-safety patterns
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using `fixedRate` for a slow task (overlaps pile up) or forgetting distributed locking in a cluster
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss `TaskScheduler` sizing, async + scheduled, error handlers, ShedLock vs Quartz tradeoffs, cron pitfalls (timezones, DST, Spring 6-field vs Unix 5-field)

fixedRate vs fixedDelay vs cron Timing
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
    note["Each row shows successive runs of one @Scheduled method"]
    fr1["fixedRate=5s | Run 1 at 0s"]

    fr2 --> fr3["Run 3 at 10s (overlap risk)"]
    fd1["fixedDelay=5s | Run 1 starts 0s, ends 3s"]
```

sections.title: fixedRate vs fixedDelay vs cron — Picking the Right One
sections.content:
Each timing mode has distinct semantics. Pick by what should happen when the task takes longer than the interval.

**`fixedRate` — clock-based, start-to-start**
- Next run starts `N ms` after the previous run **start**
- If task takes longer than `N`, the next run is queued; **may overlap** with multi-thread pool
- Good for steady-cadence sampling, polling, heartbeats
- Default single-thread pool serializes tasks — drift, not true overlap

**`fixedDelay` — end-to-next-start**
- Next run starts `N ms` after the previous run **ends**
- **Never overlaps**
- Good for tasks of unpredictable duration; avoids piling up on slow external services
- Safer default than `fixedRate` for most use cases

**`cron` — time-of-day expressions**
- Spring's cron format is **6 fields**: `second minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week`
- Set `zone` explicitly — defaults to JVM local time

**Cron examples:**
- `0 0 2 * * *` — every day at 02:00
- `0 */15 * * * *` — every 15 minutes
- `0 0 12 * * MON-FRI` — noon on weekdays
- `0 30 9 15 * *` — 15th of each month at 09:30

**Macros (Spring 5.3+):**
- `@yearly`, `@monthly`, `@weekly`, `@daily`, `@hourly`

**Externalize schedules for non-redeploy changes**

```java
@Scheduled(cron = "${jobs.reporting.cron}")
public void report() { }
```

```yaml
jobs:
  reporting:
    cron: "0 0 2 * * *"
```

Use `cron = "-"` to disable a task via config.

**Cron pitfalls**
- **Spring 6-field vs Unix 5-field** — leading seconds field; common migration bug
- **Timezone** — `zone = "America/New_York"` is DST-aware; UTC is stable; prefer UTC for infra schedules
- **`*` in day-of-month and day-of-week** — both `*` means 'every day' (no AND); one `*` and one specific can surprise
- **Feb 29** — `0 0 0 29 2 *` runs every four years; use `0 0 0 L 2 *` for last day of February

sections.title: TaskScheduler Configuration — Do This Early
Making @Scheduled Safe in a Cluster
sections.content:
With N replicas running the same code, every `@Scheduled` method fires N times. For 'send nightly report' that means N emails.

**Option 1 — ShedLock (lightweight DB lock)**

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>net.javacrumbs.shedlock</groupId>
    <artifactId>shedlock-spring</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>net.javacrumbs.shedlock</groupId>
    <artifactId>shedlock-provider-jdbc-template</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

```java
@EnableScheduling
@EnableSchedulerLock(defaultLockAtMostFor = "10m")
@Configuration
public class SchedConfig {
    @Bean
    public LockProvider lockProvider(DataSource ds) {
        return new JdbcTemplateLockProvider(ds);
    }
}

@Component
public class Reports {
    @Scheduled(cron = "0 0 2 * * *", zone = "UTC")
    @SchedulerLock(name = "nightlyReport", lockAtLeastFor = "1m", lockAtMostFor = "30m")
    public void send() { }
}
```

- First replica grabs the named lock; others see it taken and skip
- `lockAtMostFor` is a safety net if the holder crashes
- Providers: JDBC, Mongo, Redis, Hazelcast, DynamoDB, ZooKeeper

**Option 2 — Quartz clustered mode**
- DB-backed JobStore with `isClustered=true`
- Heavier setup; richer cron semantics, misfire policies, recovery
- Standard for complex multi-job scheduling

**Option 3 — Kubernetes CronJob**

```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: nightly-report
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
            - name: report
              image: acme/report:1.2.3
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
```

- K8s creates a Pod at each tick; Pod runs and exits
- No `@Scheduled` in the application
- Best for K8s-native stacks with operational separation

**Decision rule:**
- Single replica → plain `@Scheduled`
- Multiple replicas, simple job → `@Scheduled` plus ShedLock
- Complex scheduling, dynamic schedules → Quartz clustered
- K8s-native, operational separation → Kubernetes CronJob

**Don't stack solutions** — running Quartz and `@Scheduled` doing the same thing produces duplicates. Pick one scheduler.

sections.title: When @Scheduled Helps, When It Hurts
sections.content:
**When `@Scheduled` helps:**
- Single-instance deployments
- Simple periodic tasks (heartbeat, cache refresh, polling)
- 80% of 'run something every 5 minutes' needs
- Zero extra infrastructure

**When `@Scheduled` hurts:**
- Multi-replica deployments without distributed locking
- Dynamic schedules (user-configurable)
- Long-running tasks that hold scheduler threads
- Workloads needing misfire handling, recovery, or dynamic management

**When `fixedRate` helps vs hurts:**
- Helps: steady cadence regardless of duration (sampling, polling)
- Hurts: slow tasks pile up under multi-thread pool — load amplification
- Default to `fixedDelay` unless steady cadence is the requirement

**Watch for:**
- **Default single-thread pool** — one slow task blocks all others; configure `ThreadPoolTaskScheduler` early
- **Default timezone** — JVM TZ is environment-dependent; always specify `zone`
- **`fixedRate` with slow task** — drift (single thread) or overlap (multi-thread)
- **Cluster duplicates** — forgetting ShedLock/Quartz/K8s CronJob
- **Swallowed exceptions** — default `ErrorHandler` just logs; add metric/alert
- **Long tasks blocking** — delegate to async executor
- **Self-invocation pitfall** — `@Async` plus `@Scheduled` on the same bean: AOP proxy may bypass `@Async`; split across beans
- **Spring vs Unix cron** — Spring is 6 fields with leading seconds; common migration bug
- **`@EnableScheduling` in test slices** — disabled by default; test methods directly

**Keep scheduled tasks short** — a `@Scheduled` method should be a trigger, not the worker. Delegate heavy work to a queue or `Executor` and return quickly. This caps the blast radius of failure and avoids holding scheduler threads.

**Idempotency** — design every scheduled task to be safe to run twice. You'll inevitably get a failure mid-task, an accidental duplicate config, or a rolling deploy where two replicas briefly hold the lock. Idempotency keys, UPSERTs, and deduping make these survivable.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@Scheduled`** triggers methods on a timer; enable with `@EnableScheduling`.
- **`fixedRate`** = N ms between start times; can overlap with multi-thread pool.
- **`fixedDelay`** = N ms between end and next start; never overlaps.
- **`cron`** = Spring's 6-field format; always set `zone` explicitly.
- **Default thread pool is single-threaded** — configure `ThreadPoolTaskScheduler` early.
- **In clusters, `@Scheduled` fires on every replica** — use ShedLock, Quartz clustered, or K8s CronJob.
- **Keep tasks short, idempotent, observable** — duration and outcome metrics, MDC logging.
- **Externalize cron via properties** — use `@ConditionalOnProperty` or `cron = "-"` to disable per environment.
- **Graceful shutdown** — `setWaitForTasksToCompleteOnShutdown(true)`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring's `@Scheduled` is the simplest way to run a method on a timer inside one JVM.

**Three timing modes:**
- `fixedRate` — N ms between start times; can overlap with multi-thread pool
- `fixedDelay` — N ms between end and next start; never overlaps
- `cron` — time-of-day expressions; Spring's 6-field format with leading seconds

**Two pitfalls everyone hits:**
- Default thread pool is single-threaded; multiple scheduled methods queue up
- Configure `ThreadPoolTaskScheduler` with `setPoolSize(10)`, error handler, graceful shutdown
- In multi-replica deployments every replica fires — duplicate runs without coordination

**Cluster-safe options:**
- ShedLock — `@Scheduled` plus `@SchedulerLock(name, lockAtMostFor, lockAtLeastFor)`; backed by JDBC/Redis/Mongo
- Quartz clustered — heavier; rich misfire and recovery semantics
- Kubernetes CronJob — schedules outside the app; Pod runs and exits at each tick

**Cron pitfalls to call out:**
- Spring 6-field vs Unix 5-field — leading seconds field; common migration bug
- Timezone — `zone = "UTC"` for stable infra schedules; named zones are DST-aware
- `*` in day-of-month and day-of-week is 'every day' (no AND semantics)
- Feb 29 — use `L 2 *` for last day of February, not `29 2 *`

**Operational hygiene:**
- Keep tasks short — delegate heavy work to a queue/Executor; method is a trigger, not the worker
- Always idempotent — failure mid-task, retries, lock expiry can cause double-runs
- Log start, end, duration, outcome with MDC
- Emit Micrometer metrics (`@Timed` or manual sample); alert on missed fires (no run in 2x period)
- Wrap the body in try/catch — uncaught exceptions are logged but the run is lost

**Decision framework:**
- Single replica → plain `@Scheduled`
- Multiple replicas, simple job → `@Scheduled` plus ShedLock
- Complex scheduling or dynamic schedules → Quartz clustered
- K8s-native, operational separation → Kubernetes CronJob
- Don't stack solutions — pick one scheduler

In an interview I'd emphasize that `@Scheduled` is great for in-process periodic work, but the moment you have more than one replica or need recovery semantics, graduate to ShedLock or Quartz.

questions.question: How do you make Spring `@Scheduled` tasks observable and resilient in production? What patterns prevent silent failures, missed fires, and runaway threads?
questions.title: @Scheduled Observability, Error Handling, and Resilience Patterns
questions.direct_answer: Production `@Scheduled` tasks need three layers of safety. **Observability** — log start/end/duration/outcome with MDC, emit Micrometer metrics (`@Timed`), and alert on missed fires (no run in 2x period). **Error handling** — wrap the body in try/catch so a single failure doesn't lose context; configure a custom `ErrorHandler` on the `TaskScheduler` for uncaught exceptions; record failure metrics and structured logs. **Resilience** — keep tasks short, delegate heavy work to a queue or `Executor`, set `setWaitForTasksToCompleteOnShutdown(true)` for graceful K8s shutdown, and protect against runaway threads via `lockAtMostFor` (ShedLock) or per-task timeouts.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can operationalize scheduled tasks beyond just declaring `@Scheduled`
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Relying on default `ErrorHandler` that just logs, with no alert on consecutive failures or missed fires
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss missed-fire detection via heartbeat metric, runaway-thread protection, and the self-invocation pitfall when combining `@Async` with `@Scheduled`

sections.title: Production Scheduled Tasks Need Three Layers — Observability, Error Handling, Resilience
sections.content:
A `@Scheduled` annotation is a single line that triggers a method on a timer. Making it production-grade is significantly more work, and the gaps are usually invisible until something breaks.

**Three layers of safety:**
- **Observability** — answer 'is this task running, how long does it take, when did it last succeed?' from operational dashboards
- **Error handling** — distinguish transient failures from real ones; record context for debugging; alert on consecutive failures
- **Resilience** — survive long-running tasks, K8s SIGTERM, runaway threads, and partial failures without halting the entire scheduler

**The common production failures:**
- Task throws silently every run for a week — no one notices because the default `ErrorHandler` just logs
- Slow task holds a scheduler thread for hours, blocking all other scheduled methods
- Lock not released because the holder crashed — no one runs the task until manual intervention
- K8s rolling deploy kills mid-task — partial state in DB, no idempotency guard
- Cron fires at unexpected time after DST transition — logs say 'ran at 03:00' instead of expected '02:00'

Every one of these is preventable with the patterns below.

sections.title: Observability — Logging, Metrics, and Missed-Fire Detection
Error Handling — Custom ErrorHandler and Failure Metrics
Resilience — Runaway Threads, Graceful Shutdown, and the @Async Pitfall
Patterns by Failure Mode
sections.content:
Map the failure mode you're protecting against to the right pattern.

| Failure Mode | Pattern |
|---|---|
| Task throws silently every run | Per-method try/catch + failure metric + alert on consecutive failures |
| No run in 2x expected period | Heartbeat metric + Prometheus alert on staleness |
| Slow task blocks scheduler | Delegate to dedicated `Executor`; configure `ThreadPoolTaskScheduler` pool size |
| K8s SIGTERM kills mid-task | `setWaitForTasksToCompleteOnShutdown(true)` + `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` |
| Crashed holder leaves lock | ShedLock `lockAtMostFor` releases lock after timeout |
| Cluster duplicate runs | ShedLock, Quartz clustered, or K8s CronJob |
| Self-invocation bypasses `@Async` | Split `@Scheduled` and `@Async` across separate beans |

sections.title: When to Add Each Layer of Safety
sections.content:
**When observability investments pay off:**
- Tasks critical to business (billing, reporting, settlement)
- Tasks called by downstream systems that depend on freshness
- Tasks where silent failure is invisible until the next business cycle

**When observability is overkill:**
- Dev-only tasks
- Tasks with obvious immediate side effects (sending notifications visible in UI)
- Throwaway one-off scripts

**When custom error handling helps:**
- Multi-tenant scheduled tasks where one tenant's failure shouldn't halt others
- Tasks with distinct transient vs permanent failure modes
- Production environments with on-call rotations needing actionable alerts

**When custom error handling hurts:**
- Simple jobs where the default logger is enough
- Adding complexity that obscures the actual work

**When delegation to executor helps:**
- Tasks that take more than a few seconds
- Tasks that loop over N items each doing real work
- Workloads where you want to throttle concurrency separately from scheduling cadence

**When delegation hurts:**
- Trivially fast tasks (heartbeat, cache refresh)
- Tasks where the indirection adds debugging complexity

**Watch for:**
- **Default `ErrorHandler`** — silent log; no alert
- **No heartbeat metric** — missed fires invisible until business impact appears
- **Self-invocation pitfall** — `@Async` on the same bean as `@Scheduled` does nothing
- **No graceful shutdown** — K8s SIGTERM mid-task corrupts state
- **No runaway protection** — stuck task holds scheduler thread forever
- **Synchronous heavy work in scheduled method** — blocks all other scheduled tasks

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Three layers** — observability, error handling, resilience.
- **Structured logging with MDC** — `taskName`, `runId` propagate through the call stack.
- **Micrometer metrics** — `scheduled.task.duration` and `scheduled.task.runs` with `outcome` tag.
- **Heartbeat metric** for missed-fire detection — alert when no success in 2x expected period.
- **Custom `ErrorHandler` on TaskScheduler** — logs and emits failure metric; default just logs.
- **Delegate heavy work to an `Executor`** — scheduler thread stays free.
- **Graceful shutdown** — `setWaitForTasksToCompleteOnShutdown(true)` plus K8s `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`.
- **`@Async` + `@Scheduled` self-invocation pitfall** — split across beans to engage the AOP proxy.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Production `@Scheduled` tasks need three layers of safety beyond the bare annotation.

**Observability:**
- Structured logging with MDC — `taskName`, `runId`, `triggeredBy` propagate through the stack
- Micrometer metrics — `scheduled.task.duration` and `scheduled.task.runs` with `outcome` tag
- Heartbeat metric — emit on every successful run; Prometheus alert on staleness (no success in 2x expected period)
- Distributed tracing via `@Observed` to correlate with downstream calls

**Error handling:**
- Wrap the method body in try/catch — preserve MDC, emit failure metric, log with context
- Custom `ErrorHandler` on the `TaskScheduler` for uncaught exceptions — default just logs
- Distinguish transient from permanent failures — different alert thresholds
- Never silently swallow — even 'expected' exceptions deserve a metric

**Resilience:**
- Delegate heavy work to a dedicated `Executor` — scheduled method runs in milliseconds, finds work, dispatches
- Graceful K8s shutdown — `setWaitForTasksToCompleteOnShutdown(true)` plus `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`
- Runaway-thread protection — ShedLock `lockAtMostFor`, per-task timeouts, or circuit breakers

**The @Async + @Scheduled pitfall:**
- `@Async` works via AOP proxy; calling `this.asyncMethod()` bypasses it
- A `@Scheduled` method calling `this.heavyWorkAsync()` does NOT run async
- Split across two beans — `TriggerScheduler` with `@Scheduled` calling `HeavyWorker.runAsync()`

**Common production failures these patterns prevent:**
- Task throws silently for a week — no one notices because default error handler just logs
- Slow task blocks the scheduler thread, delaying all other scheduled methods
- Lock not released after holder crash — task halted until manual intervention
- K8s rolling deploy kills mid-task without graceful shutdown
- Cron fires at unexpected time after DST transition

**Testing tips:**
- `@EnableScheduling` is disabled in test slices — test method directly
- Verify cron: `CronExpression.parse(...).next(Instant.now())`
- Integration tests simulate time advancement

In an interview I'd emphasize the heartbeat metric — that's the single best safety net for catching silent failures.

steps: Operational dashboards must answer four questions: is the task running, how long does it take, when did it last succeed, and when did it last fail.

Structured logging with MDC ``java @Component public class ReportingTask { private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(ReportingTask.class); private final ReportingService service; private final MeterRegistry meter; @Scheduled(cron = "0 0 2 *", zone = "UTC") public void runDailyReport() { String runId = UUID.randomUUID().toString(); MDC.put("taskName", "dailyReport"); MDC.put("runId", runId); Timer.Sample sample = Timer.start(meter); log.info("Scheduled task starting"); try { service.generateAndSend(); sample.stop(meter.timer("scheduled.task.duration", "task", "dailyReport", "outcome", "success")); meter.counter("scheduled.task.runs", "task", "dailyReport", "outcome", "success").increment(); log.info("Scheduled task completed"); } catch (Exception e) { sample.stop(meter.timer("scheduled.task.duration", "task", "dailyReport", "outcome", "failure")); meter.counter("scheduled.task.runs", "task", "dailyReport", "outcome", "failure").increment(); log.error("Scheduled task failed", e); throw e; } finally { MDC.clear(); } } } ` Heartbeat metric for missed-fire detection Emit a counter or last-success-timestamp every successful run Prometheus alert: time().
